Peppermint Mocha Pistachio Milk, Olive Wood Steak Knives, and More Things BA Editors Loved in November

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As people who write about food and kitchen gadgets for a living, Bon Appétit editors are constantly surrounded by a wide range of products.
  • This month, holiday-ready martini glasses, turmeric-laced bone broth, and digestion-friendly tea.
  • Read on for all the products we obsessed over in November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As people who write about food and kitchen gadgets for a living, Bon Appétit editors are constantly surrounded by a wide range of products. Between our own purchases and the endless stream of samples sent our way, it means there’s always something newly introduced coming across our desks and into our homes. Each month we round up the standouts we tested or bought ourselves that changed the way we cook and eat.

This month, holiday-ready martini glasses, turmeric-laced bone broth, and digestion-friendly tea.

Read on for all the products we obsessed over in November.

In a recent development, this summer, I spent a week in Paris with my family and gloriously found myself eating steak frites on more than one occasion. Besides the perfectly cooked bavette and thin, crisp fries, I was enamored with the bistro aesthetic—down to the super-sharp and sleek steak knives I used for each meal. When I came across Made In Cookware’s set, I knew it was a sign that I, too, could adopt this sophisticated French look. These knives are manufactured in Thiers, France, a region known for knife-making, which speaks to their aesthetic and craftsmanship. I love that they’re non-serrated; the sharp edges maintain the integrity of meat and can be sharpened once dull. These steak knives are also full tang, which means they’re constructed with a single rod of stainless steel from tip to handle. And speaking of the handle—the feature that attracted me to this set in the first place—they come in several materials, including olive wood, black polymer, and (my pick) pearlescent acetate. — Melissa Knific, contributing editor.

What is a martini glass if not a tiny birdbath for my olives? These Year and Day glasses are my favorite kind: classic and elevated, but durable. They’re great for anything you’d serve up, and the best part is that I can set them in the dishwasher at the end of the night. —Casey Hendricks, executive director of audience development.

Industry observers note that A woman in her late 20s who starts her mornings with a mug of bone broth as the weather gets cold—I know I’m a cliché. But this chicken bone broth from Fond, specifically the turmeric and black pepper variety, truly does start my day off on the right note. There’s eight grams of protein per cup, sure, but my favorite part is that it’s made without alliums (like garlic and onion) so it’s especially kind to my tummy. Instead, the broth gets its flavor from carrots, turmeric root, celery, lemon juice, cracked black pepper, and thyme. All the vegetables Fond uses are organic and they use 100% pasture-raised chicken, so it’s as close to making my own bone broth at home as I can get, without having to simmer a pot for 18 hours. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

M6HG Instant Hot Countertop Reverse Osmosis Water Filter.

There were a couple of things happening at my house at the same time: First, my wife’s lovely and enormous collection of houseplants continued growing; second, we decided to get a water softener to fight against the notoriously hard water in my part of Fresh Jersey. Those two things don’t go together well because softened water and its added sodium can be bad for plants long term. A reverse osmosis system is one way to fight against that, but we didn’t have the budget (or really the need) for a whole-home RO system, nor did we have the space under our sink for one of those. Enter Waterdrop’s countertop RO. The M6HG has an autofilling pitcher that makes plant care convenient, but it’s also turned out it’s getting more use than our fridge filter for drinking. Water comes out a chilly 48 degrees and measures precisely to 4, 8, or 16 ounces (which my kids love for some reason). It also dispenses at 77℉, 113℉ (supposedly good for baby formula), 131℉, 149℉, 167℉, 185℉ (for delicate tea), and 203℉ (for French press or pour-over coffee). Oh yeah, it’s on big sale for Black Friday. — Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor.

It has been revealed that I never grew up with advent calendars, but I can totally see what the fuss is about. My family and I take such joy opening up a window of surprise every morning. Since the advent calendars in our home are usually food-related, we’ll enjoy the treat together later in the evening, with varying degrees of jostling, depending on what it is. Well, looks like the 2026 holiday season will be another one of us throwing elbows because we have our hands on BonBon’s magnificent Lighthouse Advent Calendar. No paper windows here! The cool Swedish confectionary’s calendar is actually a long tower filled with 24 individually wrapped, numbered mini bags of vegan gummies. The daily candy should be a mix of BonBon’s exclusive upcoming flavors as well as its beloved classics. I think my Swedish husband and daughter are already losing their minds (it’s only November) and I’m already fearing for our next dental visit, but it is giving this exceptionally fast holiday season a good reason to stop and appreciate a fun, sweet moment every day. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food director.

In a recent development, ’Tis the season for...soup. My Dutch oven and I have been on a tear making favorites like white chicken chili, chicken-lentil soup, and tons of minestrone. In my attempt to “be frugal,” I’ve been bringing my soups to work for lunch in my, yes, ludicrously capacious bag, and more specifically, my 20 oz. insulated thermos by Hydroflask. It’s truly the perfect size for a lunch-appropriate portion and keeps my soup warm from morning until around 1 p.m. when it’s time to eat between meetings. It’s completely leak-proof which is crucial for a soup commute. And, it’s dishwasher safe, so when I come home after work, I can just throw it in the dishwasher to use all over again the next day. A small investment for a considerably more delightful desk lunch. —June Kim, executive editor.

Limited Edition Peppermint Mocha Barista.

I’m not really a pumpkin spice latte girl, but a peppermint mocha is a seasonal drink I can definitely get behind—so when I heard that Táche, the brand behind my favorite pistachio milk, had come out with a Peppermint Mocha flavor, I was very eager to try it. Sure enough, it was love at first sip. It tastes deeply chocolatey thanks to the addition of Dutch-processed cocoa, and has just enough peppermint flavor to feel festive and balanced without veering into toothpaste territory. I’ve been mixing it with a shot of espresso over ice to make an easy peppermint mocha latte, but to be honest with you, my favorite way to enjoy it is straight up, chilled and poured into a glass. —Alaina Chou, commerce writer.

Recent findings suggest that I’m often hesitant to use pre-made, packaged products when it comes to cooking. One could say I’m a bit of a control freak, but I’m not opposed to a shortcut, especially when it’s after 7 p.m. on a weeknight and I still need to get dinner on the table.

Industry observers note that enter Gymkhana Butter Masala Mild Simmer Sauce. The London-based, two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant recently rolled out a line of sauces, marinades, and chutneys inspired by its iconic dishes. I paired the butter masala sauce with cubed paneer that I rapidly broiled, topped everything with fresh cilantro, and served it alongside basmati rice.

The sauce is rich, complex, and packed with flavor, yet all it requires is a quick reheat. Dinner came together in less than 30 minutes and tasted like something I’d order at a restaurant. Needless to say, I’ll be stocking up on a few more jars. —Ali Inglese, executive producer.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve absolutely been loving this soothing tisane (aka herbal tea!) from La Vie tea. Produced in the French tradition—and primarily sourced directly from French gardens!—these delicate blends are all made from herbs, flowers, and spices as opposed to tea leaves. The digestion-friendly blend I’ve been enjoying is mostly ginger, fennel, and chamomile, with notes of orange and cinnamon—I’ve been parked on the couch with a huge mug of this brew after many a hearty dinner this month. I’m looking forward to dipping into the lavender-scented “Calm” blend ahead of the forthcoming hectic holiday season! —Rebecca Firkser, test kitchen editor.

According to recent reports, I’m a complete nut for ice cream. Regardless of the season, I’m always ready to pop a pint open for dessert (or a mid-day pick-me-up, let’s be honest). And I can say unequivocally that Graeter’s is my favorite ice cream of all time. Even Oprah agrees with me. She named it her favorite too back in 2002. And thanks to the modern miracle that is dry ice, you can have the best ice cream on the planet sent straight to your door. This option is available year-round, allowing you to pick your own flavors in packs of six or twelve pints (get the Coconut Chip if you know what’s good for you). But if you want to get in the holiday spirit, start with the Holiday Pack. It offers an assortment of seasonal flavors as well as the always in-demand, Black Raspberry Chip. Whether you’re treating yourself this year or shopping for that impossible-to-buy-for friend, this small-batch ice cream from the Buckeye State is the way to go. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy.

They have a perfectly crunchy exterior and are filled with all of our favorite Thanksgiving dishes: leftover turkey, mashed potatoes, cranberries, and stuffing. It’s the perfect way to use up every last bite of those beloved leftovers—here’s how to make them:.

It has been revealed that making Thanksgiving egg rolls:The key to keeping your egg rolls together when frying? Don’t overstuff them. Is It Rude to Bring Your Own Food to Thanksgiving?

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.
  • In a recent development, thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year.
  • It has been revealed that for the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host indicates dinner is ready.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.

In a recent development, thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

It has been revealed that for the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host indicates dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

It has been revealed that once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

The short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

According to recent reports, A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:.

I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a big breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

Recent findings suggest that I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

First, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a big deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

This is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really important to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

And I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really vital for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

It’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

Sources indicate that thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

Breaking: Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • In a recent development, crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

In a recent development, crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, New York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

Industry observers note that while there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, remarked that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

According to recent reports, wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

Industry observers note that part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit New York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she claims. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

Sources indicate that A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Industry observers note that spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, claims that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to new takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she says. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

  • The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.
  • Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

In a recent development, rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she noted when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”.

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, remarked she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

Sources indicate that “Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had stated they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that the two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack stated she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”.

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this matter.”.

It has been revealed that leger Fernández noted if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

Recent findings suggest that “We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández noted. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”.

Giant Sheet-Pan Chocolate Almond Croissant

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant has a filling of frangipane and melted chocolate chips between two light, buttery sheets of puff pastry.
  • This giant croissant is practically the size of a sheet pan.
  • According to recent reports, preheat the oven to 425°F.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Our giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant has a filling of frangipane and melted chocolate chips between two light, buttery sheets of puff pastry.

This giant croissant is practically the size of a sheet pan. The bigger, the better, as they say, but we’re more into its shareable nature and simple-to-make design. Shatteringly crisp puff pastry (store-bought, of course) replaces hard-to-make croissant dough, with extra square footage for both this treat’s iconic croissant fillings: pain au chocolat and almond croissant. Win-win-win. Save this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant for special occasions or holiday mornings.

According to recent reports, preheat the oven to 425°F. On a lightly floured surface, roll out each sheet of puff pastry to a 12×10-inch rectangle. Place one on a parchment-lined 15x10x1-inch baking pan. Top the puff pastry with a second piece of parchment paper and a second 15x10x1-inch baking pan. This keeps the puff pastry from rising too much so it stays flat.

Bake the puff pastry for 15 minutes. Remove the top pan and parchment. Continue baking the puff pastry until it’s golden brown, five to seven minutes longer. Cool the puff pastry on a wire rack. Repeat the same process with the second slice of puff pastry.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, in a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, almond flour and confectioners’ sugar until they’re light and fluffy, two to three minutes. Add the egg and beat well until it’s incorporated.

Place one baked sheet of puff pastry on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Spread two-thirds of the almond filling over it.

Sprinkle the chocolate chips evenly all over. Carefully place the second sheet of baked puff pastry over top, and pipe or spread the remaining third of the almond filling on top.

Sprinkle the top with sliced almonds.

Industry observers note that reduce the oven setting to 350°. Bake the croissant just until the filling is set, 18 to 20 minutes longer. Cool the croissant completely on a wire rack before serving.

Just as you’re ready to serve, dust the top with confectioners’ sugar and, if desired, drizzle it with warm hot fudge.

Store leftover giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant in an airtight container in the fridge. It can be kept for up to three days. Just know that it is best enjoyed the day of, as the frangipane will make the puff pastry soggy.

It has been revealed that yes, you can make certain aspects of a giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant ahead of time, but wait to assemble and bake it until you’re ready to serve. You can bake the puff pastry sheets one day ahead, let them cool to room temperature, wrap them tightly in storage wrap and store them at room temperature. Make the frangipane up to two days beforehand and keep it covered in the fridge.

Recent findings suggest that yes, you can make a gluten-free version of this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant. Simply replace the puff pastry with a gluten-free variety. DuFour, Sweet Loren’s and Schar make fantastic gluten-free puff pastry. All other ingredients are naturally gluten free (but do double-check the hot fudge, if you’re using it); just make sure they weren’t processed in a facility that handles wheat.

Serve your giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant with strong coffee or tea. Pair it with other brunch, like egg casseroles, plates of bacon and sausage and a fruit salad. I wouldn’t set out any other sweets—this croissant is plenty!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from stated anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

It has been revealed that cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that I have a confession to make.
  • I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It has been revealed that I thought I knew exactly how I felt about ranch dressing. Then I made Ina's version.

It has been revealed that I have a confession to make. I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing. I realize this puts me at odds with a substantial portion of the American population, but I’ve always preferred a good balsamic vinaigrette or a creamy Caesar. And despite making countless salad dressings over the years, I’ve never once felt compelled to make ranch.

I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch. I found the whole business unappealing, an opinion that has apparently skipped a generation seeing as both of my children now do exactly the same thing. There’s always a bottle of ranch in our refrigerator that was purchased specifically for pizza night, and it has absolutely nothing to do with me.

Recent findings suggest that then I came across an Instagram reel of Ina Garten making her buttermilk ranch dressing for a wedge salad. I’ve trusted Ina with everything from roast chicken to panna cotta, and if anyone could persuade me to reconsider my longstanding position on ranch, I figured it would be her. So, after decades of avoiding it, I finally made a batch of ranch dressing.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Ina’s recipe makes about 3 cups of dressing, which initially struck me as an ambitious quantity for someone with my history of distatte. Fortunately, it comes together in just a few minutes, and the ingredients are far more fresh and interesting than anything I’d previously associated with ranch.

Combine the scallions, basil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, olive oil, garlic, salt and pepper in a food processor fitted with a steel blade. Puree them for 15 to 20 seconds, until the mixture is smooth.

It has been revealed that add the mayonnaise, Greek yogurt and buttermilk, then blend the dressing again until everything is thoroughly combined. Transfer the dressing to a covered container and refrigerate it for an hour to let the flavors develop.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

That’s really all there is to it. No complicated technique or careful emulsifying, and very little cleanup. The hour in the refrigerator is notable, though, since it gives the garlic, herbs and other seasonings time to mingle with the creamy ingredients.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, of course, I expected Ina’s ranch to be better than the bottled varieties I’ve tried. What I didn’t expect was for it to taste like an entirely different dressing.

It has been revealed that the first thing that struck me was how fresh it was. The basil and scallions give it a wonderful, almost garden-like quality, while the garlic and Dijon add savory sharpness that keeps all that creaminess interesting. There’s plenty of richness from the mayonnaise, but the buttermilk, Greek yogurt and lemon juice provide enough acidity to balance it. It’s tangy, herbaceous and wonderfully flavorful—without the heavy, slightly cloying quality I’ve always associated with ranch.

Recent findings suggest that and the basil! It’s not an herb I would have thought to put in ranch dressing, but it works beautifully. Its flavor comes through clearly without overwhelming the other ingredients, giving the dressing a character all its own.

In her video, Ina serves the dressing over a wedge salad topped with tomatoes and onion. Having already entrusted her with the dressing, I figured I might as well follow her lead with the salad, too. I made my own wedge with Flavor Bombs tomatoes (my favorites), pepitas and crispy pieces of bacon, then spooned a generous amount of ranch over the whole thing. The cold, crunchy lettuce was the perfect backdrop for the dressing, while the sweet tomatoes, salty bacon and nutty pepitas made the whole thing particularly satisfying. I’ve always loved a good wedge salad, but this was easily one of the best I’ve had.

By the time I’d finished testing and photographing the recipe, nearly half the dressing was gone, and I was already making looks for the rest. I have to admit, I’m even curious to see how it tastes with pizza, which is not something I ever expected to say about ranch dressing.

Turkey stock is a must-make if you had turkey as your Thanksgiving centerpiece. You don't want to let those scraps go to waste, do you? Throw in some of those wilting herbs and whatever carrots and celery you have on hand to make a great pantry staple. It takes almost zero effort and leaves you with a flavorful stock that you can store in the freezer until you're ready to put it to use.

You can make basically anything you'd make with chicken stock (which is a lot!) with this stock. One of the best uses of turkey stock is turkey gravy and that can be used to top something like poutine or stuffing. Or you can make a time-tested classic Turkey Tetrazzini. Whatever you do, don't let this stock go to waste.

In a recent development, add all of the ingredients to a large stockpot. Cover turkey completely with water, about 10 to 12 cups.

Sources indicate that over medium heat, bring the stockpot to a boil, then reduce heat and let it simmer for 3 hours. Spoon fat off the top as it rises.

Use tongs to remove the turkey carcass.

Strain stock through a fine mesh strainer. Let the stock cool to room temperature.

Store in refrigerator until ready to use for up to 2 weeks or in the freezer for 3 months.

Stock is the perfect thing to store in your freezer! After letting your stock cool to room temp you can store in the refrigerator for 2 weeks or in the freezer for up to 3 months. Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Recent findings suggest that calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

According to recent reports, one incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

It has been revealed that two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

No ricotta? Reach for a scoop of protein-rich cottage cheese. It's the secret to these tender, moist and protein-rich meatballs.

My kids have never been huge meat eaters. In fact, my son is more likely to polish off a giant bowl of cherry tomatoes than he is to dig into a burger. Meatballs, though, have always been the exception—and these cottage cheese meatballs have been a long-time favorite. My kids love how tender and juicy they are, and I love that they sneak a little extra protein into their diet.

Many traditional meatball recipes already include ricotta cheese, which binds and adds moisture to the meat mixture. Cottage cheese is a natural swap, adding fat that keeps the meatballs irresistibly moist and tender. Once these protein-packed meatballs are simmered in your favorite jarred pasta sauce and served over pasta, people will never guess that cottage cheese is the secret ingredient.

Editor’s Tip: For the softest, most tender meatballs, handle them gently as you shape them. Avoid overhandling or compacting the meat too much (one of Grandma’s best meatball tips), as it can make the meatballs tough and dense.

A crispier, more substantial coating could make McDonald’s a much stronger competitor to chains like Popeyes and Chick-fil-A.

Rolling out hand-breaded chicken across thousands of restaurants, however, is easier said than done.

Industry observers note that the reported tests are designed to evaluate customer demand, preparation costs, and how the additional steps could affect kitchen operations. Some franchisees have reportedly expressed concerns about increased labor requirements and potential kitchen renovations.

Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

📅 28 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon.
  • Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp.
  • According to recent reports, I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 matter of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

According to recent reports, I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Recent findings suggest that absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

Recent findings suggest that IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

According to recent reports, IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Try as we might, there’s just no changing the hearts and minds of some people, even our dearest loved ones, by presenting them with inconvenient truths. I’m talking, of course, about people who prefer coffee from pods. But based on the popularity of coffee pod machines, it seems those of us who haven’t been assimilated into pod people are outnumbered. And, to be fair, even if the quality of their coffee is all over the place, we can’t deny their convenience. My goal here is to find single-serve coffee makers that can blend that convenience with coffee I actually want to drink.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to plastic and aluminum pods, there’s a bevy of grounds-based coffee makers that specialize in one-cup-at-a-time brewing. So if you’re interested in the ease of pod machines, low-volume coffee brewing for one, or just can’t avoid K-cups, here are the machines that brewed the best.

Industry observers note that thanks to the revival of pour-over and French press coffee making and the proliferation of chic matte-finish electric kettles, there are plenty of ways to brew a single cup of coffee without a dedicated machine and, in general, they give you better results. We will also note that many fancier drip coffee makers (like our favorites from Fellow and Oxo) can now be programmed to brew just one cup of coffee at a time—and do so without the plastic waste of pods. If you want true versatility and have the counter space, we’d advise you to consider a machine that will let you brew for yourself or a crowd, if needed. But we understand the convenience factor of capsule machines, which is why, if you must pop a pod for your daily cup, we’ve made our recommendations below, plus suggested some non-pod options too.

Updated 11/25/26: Nespresso is phasing out it's old Vertuo Plus machines but never fear, the fresh Vertuo Up is an even better version of the original and it's our new top pick. And in other news, Keurig released its first completely K-Cup-free machine, and the new Alta platform is really quite good. That makes it the first Keurig machine we've ever recommended.

Vertuo Plus Coffee and Espresso Maker by Breville.

Caffeinator Single-Serve Coffee Maker.

Custom Grind & Brew Single Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 5” x 18" x 10.5”Water reservoir capacity: 47 oz.Colors: 4Coffee sizes: 1.3 oz., 2.7 oz., 5 oz., 8 oz., 12 oz., 18 oz.

Industry observers note that what we love: Everything we loved about the original Nespresso Vertuo machine is present in the Vertuo Up. The centrifugal brewing method patented for Vertuo machines makes more balanced, better extracted coffee than most typical pod and capsule methods that just shower the grounds with water. And Nespresso continues to expand the world of capsules you can use, now featuring a number of single origin pods for those who prefer flavor profiles from different growing regions around the world, as well as flavored pods for folks whose regular Starbucks order is 13 words long.

And the Vertuo system also reads whatever capsule you insert and automatically brews at the proper volume, so it really does have one-button operation.

The rotating water tank is a nice touch because it allows the machine to fit in any configuration of kitchen and it's very easy to refill.

According to recent reports, but the biggest upgrade is the addition of what Nespresso calls “Coffee Creation” mode, which is particularly good for iced coffee lovers. The extra button tells the machine to brew a more concentrated, smaller dose of coffee. That means it can melt the ice without diluting the flavor of the drink. It also lets you add a healthy pour of milk to hot coffee with the same results.

Sources indicate that what we'd leave: Nespresso pods tend towards darker, roastier coffees. So if you have a thing for fruitier, more acidic coffee, you may be better off with either something that uses whole beans or Keurig's Alta.

Size: 10.84" W × 11.77" H × 19.0" DWater reservoir capacity: 72 ouncesColors: 3Coffee sizes: 1.5 oz. to 12 oz.

Sources indicate that for a brand that’s name is pretty much synonymous with plastic pods, Keurig threw us for a loop in 2026 when it unveiled Alta, its first plastic pod-free system. Alta is still a single-serve machine and it still uses a capsule of sorts, swapping those little cups for AltaRounds, tablets of ground coffee held together by a compostable vegetable-based coating. Each AltaRound is printed with a QR code that tells the machine what drink styles it should offer up on the touchscreen display from remarked coffee, whether it is a smaller espresso tablet or a larger flavor coffee round.

In a recent development, what we love: In my experience, this is the first machine with any association to Keurig that I’ve actively enjoyed the coffee from and kept returning to. For contrast, the whole time I tested the Alta, I had my usual DeLonghi machine set up but a few feet away and for weeks I didn’t touch it because the coffee I really liked the coffee I got from the Alta. There were nuances between the different roasts, from light to medium to dark, and detectably different intensities in the espresso rounds. (Keurig’s announcement states that Peet’s coffee is already on board for future AltaRounds offerings and more partnerships are on the way.).

Customization, while usually limited to three dots indicating temperature and brew strength, was also effective, if a bit. When selecting a milk-based drink, the frother did an impressive job of adjusting to various temperatures and thicknesses, though I did find I usually had to scoop a good bit of any super airy cold foam or cappuccino foam from the pitcher with a spoon.

In a recent development, navigating the menu was clear and easy. And once I got the hang of it, I found many aspects of the Alta, like the generous 72-ounce water tank and easy to empty drip and used coffee trays, or the simple swaps from hot to iced, to be seamless and a pleasure to use.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: First, it’s a large machine at 19 inches deep, occupying significant counter space, and while part of that has to do with the milk frothing apparatus, it’s also because the AltaRounds and separate K-cup slots are side-by-side, meaning if and when the brand just made the leap to an AltaRounds-only machine, it could probably be a good bit smaller. The automatic nature of the frother is handy, but pouring my own milk in a world of automatic dispensers on super-automatic espresso machines, left it up to me to set up the milk and do the pouring which may be more work than most Keurig converted coffee drinkers are used to. The generous water tank I called out above is slightly limiting in terms of where it allows you to set the machine up. It slides in or out from the side and if you don’t have space next to your Alta to do that, this could pose a problem. I also found the pours a bit splashy, and constantly had little droplets of coffee on the machine and on the counter nearby.

The touchscreen placement is a little wonky. It’s flat on top of the machine making it a little hard to read, and it’s actually housed in the lid for the AltaRounds slot, something that a new user (or houseguest) might not realize, as the K-cup slot is more readily discoverable with no screen and a lip for lifting it up. I fully put an AltaRound into the K-cup slot on the first go around before I more carefully read the instructions. This machine connects to WiFi, which is probably important for downloading new coffee brand specs as more AltaRounds become available, but my software updates were sometimes sticky and required unplugging the machine to unfreeze it.

Lastly, just to harp on the elephant plastic pod in the room, the Alta as it stands feels like a bridge machine to something better, but because of the sheer magnitude of the K-cup world Keurig has created, we’re stuck with a hybrid that feels part past and part future.

Caffeinator Single-Serve Coffee Maker.

There’s a snazzy drip tray that slides up and down for differently sized cups, and backlit touch buttons that disappear into the satin finish exterior (in Concrete or Midnight) when not selected. In addition to looking good, it also produced a pretty good cup of coffee, both from pods and grounds thanks to three simultaneous streams of water.

Sources indicate that it offers a lot of customization possibilities, with three hot temperature options from “warm” to “piping hot” (the latter of which raised the temp about 20 degrees from default “hot”), plus a lower temp iced coffee mode, and three brew strengths in addition to multiple cup size selections. It's also compatible with both K-cups and ground coffee. All that gave me the ability to get my coffee a little closer to the way I want it, even if it comes from a plastic pod.
