According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that STEM-based schoolwork is a key part of your kid’s curriculum, but encouraging genuine enthusiasm for science, technology, engineering, and math that extends beyond the classroom requires more than a good teacher. For the right kid at the right age, a robotics kit may be a perfect fit. It can give a budding inventor the chance to learn about science in a practical way, on their own terms, and allows them to get creative. It also highlights that science can be fun, and more than just a subject at school.

A good robotics kit balances out learning and problem solving with play. Not all of them do that effectively, though: Choosing the right one for the child in your life may not be so straightforward—particularly if you’re unfamiliar with the basics that robotics kits teach. To help you find a STEM gift this holiday season that's both fun and educational, we’ve compiled a lineup of editor-approved robotics kits. Whether you're getting ahead of shopping season or looking for a great last-minute holiday gift, these toys are both fun and give your child's mind a chance to grow.

Recent findings suggest that during our research, we drew from our collective experience covering STEM toys and equipment for kids, including topics like the best microscopes and the best graphing calculators. We also read through studies on the importance of STEM education.

In a recent development, to make our selections, we looked for kits from reputable companies within the robotics space, such as Learning Resources and Wonder Workshop. We also took a look at toys and items that parents on the staff have bought for their own kids, making special note of any that ended up as household favorites.

Recent findings suggest that while evaluating each kit, we gauged value for the price (especially because some kits cost upwards of $100), the STEM topics it covers, as well as how intuitive and (just as importantly) fun it is to use, according to parents’ reviews. Furthermore, we considered a wide variety of toys to account for different kids’ interests, ages, and skill levels.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re on the search for a robot kit with a variety of play options that isn't too expensive, this is it. The solar robot toy from Sillbird includes the pieces necessary to build 12 different robot designs, so your kid will never run out of fresh ways to play.

The robotics kit offers two levels of difficulty, with half of the builds being simpler to assemble while the other half are more complex. So, once your kid masters the easier builds, they can move on to more challenging designs, all without ever needing a new toy.

Sources indicate that A unique feature of this robot in particular is its power source. Instead of burning through heaps of batteries like other robot toys, it relies exclusively on an integrated solar panel that sits on the robot’s head. Whenever it slows down, simply place it in some sunshine and wait for it to recharge.

You can always count on Lego to be fun and engaging, but this kit throws in some coding and robotics to the classic building experience. This 1,177-piece set includes three Lego Star Wars droids—R2-D2, a Gonk Droid, and a Mouse Droid. Each of the droids looks like a standard Lego creation, but is designed to hold color and distance sensors, as well as an interactive motor.

Once they're built, kids can use the free Lego Boost smartphone app to program their droids and give them 40 different coding missions. Lego Boost is available on iOS, Android, Kindle, and Windows 10 devices.

With additional pieces included in the kit, kids can build and attach tools and weapons directly onto the droid for extra fun as they play.

Recent findings suggest that this 77-piece activity set is reasonably priced and is perfect for beginners to coding and robotics. Botley the Coding Robot comes to life with an easy-to-use remote, so there are no apps to download (and no screen time involved). All coding is done directly on the remote control and Botley can be programmed to follow up to 120 steps in a row.

The kit includes coding activity sheets to help beginners learn the basics and get the most out of their robot. The kit also comes with several fun accessories, including black line pieces that Botley can follow on its own like a track, as well as several cubes and rods you can use to build obstacle courses.

Industry observers note that for parents who want to introduce young kids to coding or build confidence in their new skills, Wonder Workshop’s Dash is a smart choice for young enthusiasts. Where many kits require extensive building before they’re up and running, Dash comes fully assembled and ready for about five hours of playtime before it needs a charge.

Each Dash is programmed to respond to external stimuli, so it can recognize and respond to dancing, singing, and the sound of your voice.

Sources indicate that this coding toy is compatible with Lego, allowing kids to use it as a base for making their own Lego creations. There are also five free apps to download that give kids fun coding project ideas, from beginner concepts to more advanced ones as they gradually get the hang of programming.

It has been revealed that makeblock’s mBot is an excellent toy for young programmers looking to challenge their knowledge and electronics skills in practical application. The small robot takes about 15 minutes to build using an easy-to-follow guide and step-by-step instructions in 3D.

Kids learn to code in Scratch, a graphic programming language, with free included software. There’s also an app with game-based tasks to challenge kids and help them advance their skills.

Sources indicate that the robot itself also has several features that expand its range of capabilities, such as the line follower sensor, the infrared sensor for the remote control, and the Bluetooth chip for controlling the bot from your phone. The toy is compatible with Lego bricks and has four expansion ports where you can add additional parts later on.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot to like about this very cute little robot ball. It’s reasonably priced for what it offers, has a super-cool LED matrix that demonstrates off characters and vector graphics, and boasts a top speed of 4.5 mph. The Sphero also has built-in sensors that detect light, cardinal directions, gyroscopic direction, and speed.

It has been revealed that what makes this robot special is how it allows users to grow along with it. Once basic skills are mastered, young coders can move on to learning JavaScript, Scratch, and Swift.

Another plus is this robot toy’s durability. It’s waterproof and scratch-proof, so young explorers can take it outside through ponds and over rocks.

It has been revealed that robotics toys are, at their core, building toys. This kit from KiwiCo comes with internal motor pieces, external body parts, and blank robot skins so kids can design their own robot.

Industry observers note that the finished product uses springs and a spinning mechanism to help the robot jump forward and rotate its arms. The key reason we like this kit so much is how well it focuses on hands-on application.

Unlike other options that are based in coding and higher-level thinking, this helps kids work with their hands and see how each individual piece interacts with the other.

Recent findings suggest that coding and basic electrical engineering are the focuses of this rover from Snap Circuits. Kids are challenged to build a full circuit board piece by piece, with over 30 parts to snap together, and then attach the board to the wheeled base.

Once the rover is built, kids code commands and directions for their “missions,” including patterns of flashing lights and sounds to get into the action.

Recent findings suggest that one of the great things about this robot toy is that it takes kids from beginner to intermediate as their skills improve. After kids get a grasp of how to code through the app, they can create more advanced commands on their own using Blockly.

The robot also functions as a fun remote-control car that kids can drive in real time through the app.

Sources indicate that this kit encourages kids to build and rebuild the robots, cars, and creatures of their dreams. It’s perfect for the budding inventor who likes to tinker with things around the house. There’s even a game element—10 playing cards that challenge kids to build various creations on the spot.

It has been revealed that protective goggles and a screwdriver accompany the included wooden pieces, electric motors and batteries, and hardware and tools. All the wooden pieces fit together easily and are designed with multiple purposes in mind.

While there is no coding element to the toy, its main focus is on helping kids build creative solutions to prompts and bolster their engineering and problem-solving skills.

It has been revealed that studies show that in addition to STEM literacy, robotics can help develop core skills like hands-on creativity, problem solving, communication, and teamwork. So teaching robotics isn’t just about setting up your kid to have a career as a computer programmer or engineer—it equips them with tech know-how and critical thinking they’ll need for virtually any type of education or work.

According to recent reports, choose toys that allow your kid to use their imagination and play out multiple different situations, both real and made up. Furthermore, make sure even if you want the toy to help them learn STEM skills, it still fits their interests and passions. A toy that gets played with often will help them learn a lot more than a more educational one that collects dust.

While you may think robotics clubs are only for middle and high schoolers, research has shown that children are also able to master basic robotics and programming skills when they’re introduced in pre-K to second grade.

Many of these kits are appropriate for children as young as 3 years old, while some are more advanced with an age suggestion of 8 and up. Before you buy, check the recommended age range listed by the company or on the box to make sure you’re choosing a robotics kit that challenges your kid while still being accessible to them.

You don’t have to shell out hundreds of dollars right away on a robot, especially if your kids are still learning what they like. There are plenty of robotics kits that run under $50 if you aren’t sure your kids are going to enjoy this kind of play and learning. Pricier options over $100 offer more complexity and can often grow with the kids, since they’re customizable to continue challenging them as they get older and gain experience.

Solo meerkats can find their way back home

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.
  • It has been revealed that the animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, states Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

It has been revealed that the animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, states Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

Sources indicate that the answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she indicates. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin states.).

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin notes. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

Recent findings suggest that it’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she notes, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

Sources indicate that “I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden remarked in a social media post last week.

A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In a recent development, in the classic Dr.
  • “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” states the narrator of the 1966 movie version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, in the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

“They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” states the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really significant in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, states Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”.

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson states. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”.

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

Sources indicate that there are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson claims. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

According to recent reports, some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand says, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”.

Sources indicate that stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson notes.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

Sources indicate that so instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson claims. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.).

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as massive as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

It has been revealed that but becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”.

Big hope and lots of help for a tiny fish that lives in a desert cave

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The endangered Devils Hole pupfish rebounded to 137 fish in October 2026, following captive-bred releases and feeding after earthquake damage.
  • Biologists counted 137 Devils Hole pupfish on Oct.
  • The fall 2025 survey had found 69 fish, and the spring 2026 survey found 77, according to the National Park Service (NPS).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The endangered Devils Hole pupfish rebounded to 137 fish in October 2026, following captive-bred releases and feeding after earthquake damage.

Biologists counted 137 Devils Hole pupfish on Oct. 10, 2026, in the only place the species lives in the wild: a water-filled cavern in the Nevada desert.

The fall 2025 survey had found 69 fish, and the spring 2026 survey found 77, according to the National Park Service (NPS).

According to recent reports, devils Hole is a detached unit of Death Valley National Park. It opens onto an aquifer, and Ash Meadows is the discharge point for a groundwater system that reaches more than 100 miles (160 kilometers) to the northeast.

The cavern is more than 500 feet (152 meters) deep, and its bottom has never been mapped, according to the park’s Devils Hole page. The water stays at 92°F (33°C).

The fish forage and spawn on a shallow rock shelf near the surface, where they feed on algae and diatoms. That shelf, the population’s main feeding and breeding ground, covers about 215 square feet (20 square meters).

It has been revealed that the fish are about 1 to 1.5 inches (2.5 to 3.8 centimeters) long. Males are iridescent blue, while females are olive-green.

In a recent development, the species has been isolated for 10,000 to 20,000 years, longer than any other pupfish in the Death Valley system. A presidential proclamation added Devils Hole to what was then Death Valley National Monument in 1952.

Recent findings suggest that scuba divers and surface counters from the NPS and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) survey the fish at the same time. Divers count in the cavern’s depths, while others watch the limestone shelf.

Industry observers note that biologists have used these methods nearly every spring and fall since 1972. Through the mid-1990s, counts averaged about 200 fish in spring and 425 in fall.

Recent findings suggest that in the early 2000s, spring counts averaged about 90. The number dropped to 35 in spring 2013.

Industry observers note that pupfish numbers naturally rise and fall. The two agencies say continued monitoring, research and habitat management remain essential.

Industry observers note that two earthquakes, one in December and the other in February, set off waves in the cavern’s normally still water. The waves moved algae, organic material and fish eggs off the shelf.

Recent findings suggest that A dive in March 2025 found only 20 or so fish. The official spring 2025 count recorded 38, down from 191 one year earlier.

“The present size at near-record lows deserves our serious attention, and the actions in the strategic proposal, including supplemental feeding and population augmentation, provide the best opportunity for recovery,” Michael Schwemm, a senior fish biologist with the USFWS, remarked in April 2025.

“I’m proud of the work of this interagency team to monitor and protect the Devils Hole pupfish,” Mike Reynolds, superintendent of Death Valley National Park, noted at the time.

Sources indicate that an earthquake struck Panama, nearly 3,000 miles (4,800 kilometers) away, on Oct. 9, 2026, the day before the survey. Biologists first saw signs of stress in the fish, but a later visit found them in healthier condition.

Industry observers note that backup fish live at the Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility, built in 2013 with a Southern Nevada Public Land Management Act grant. Its refuge tank holds about 100,000 gallons (380,000 liters) and includes a replica of the Devils Hole habitat.

Sources indicate that staff collect eggs, aquatic invertebrates and algae from Devils Hole each month with NPS partners. They raise the young fish and add them to the refuge tank as young adults.

Industry observers note that in spring 2025, biologists added captive-raised fish to the wild population for the first time. In all, 72 such fish were released into Devils Hole between March 2025 and February 2026.

Teams also fed the wild fish while the algae recovered, using data from the facility and from NPS monitoring.

“We were fortunate we had a strategic initiative that allowed us to act cautiously but swiftly,” mentioned Kevin Wilson, an aquatic ecologist and Devils Hole program manager at Death Valley National Park, in May 2026. That plan guided the step of “moving the refuge tank fish to Devils Hole to assist with recovery,” he said.

Schwemm said the 2022 plan “was instrumental in ensuring the wild population’s survival.”.

The rebound followed those releases of captive-raised fish and the months of supplemental feeding in Devils Hole.

Still, the pupfish lives only 10 to 14 months on average. Biologists therefore believe most of the fish in the October count hatched and grew up in Devils Hole.

“It’s exciting to see Devils Hole pupfish numbers increase so significantly over the past year,” Reynolds said this fall.

“While challenges remain, we’re encouraged by this progress and committed to its long-term survival,” he added.

The species was listed as endangered in 1967. A 1976 court ruling in Cappaert v. United States recognized a water right for Devils Hole, and an injunction limited groundwater pumping to keep the shelf underwater.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that for about 30 years, researchers have studied corporate psychopaths.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A management researcher scored a 1629 mutiny leader against a modern corporate psychopath checklist, and he matched all ten traits.

Industry observers note that for about 30 years, researchers have studied corporate psychopaths. They are the charming, ruthless bosses who rule by fear and blame everyone else. Most of the examples that come to mind are usually living or recent executives.

Now the earliest one on record may be a merchant who ran a survivors’ camp after a 1629 wreck. Scored against a ten-item checklist built for today’s boardrooms, Jeronimus Cornelisz of the Dutch East India Manufacturer matches every item.

Clive Boddy, an associate professor of management at Anglia Ruskin University in England, wrote the paper alone. Boddy has spent years studying corporate psychopathy.

It has been revealed that this paper is a historical case study rather than an experiment. It leans mainly on the historian Mike Dash’s 2003 book about the wreck.

Other sources are the expedition commander’s journal, a pastor’s letters, trial records, and skeletons dug up on the island.

“What makes this case remarkable is that when we analyzed Cornelisz using a modern management psychopathy framework, he displayed every major characteristic associated with corporate psychopaths,” Boddy mentioned.

The Batavia was the firm’s latest flagship, bound for the port the Dutch had renamed Batavia, now Jakarta.

On the morning of June 4, 1629, it struck a reef in the Houtman Abrolhos islands. The reef lies 80 miles (130 kilometers) off Western Australia, and most of the people aboard managed to reach a small coral island.

In a recent development, somewhere between 180 and 250 people made it ashore, and 30 of them were women and children. The island had no fresh water of its own.

The commander, Francisco Pelsaert, the ship’s captain, and 46 others then left in an overloaded longboat to fetch help from Jakarta, 900 miles (1,450 kilometers) away.

That left Cornelisz, a junior merchant and the most senior company man still on the island, in charge of everyone else.

Cornelisz had been plotting a mutiny before the ship went down. Once in command, Boddy wrote, he replaced the lawful council with his fellow plotters and had them swear personal oaths of loyalty.

He moved the money chests, water, and food into his own tent, and the plan was to seize whatever rescue ship arrived and turn pirate.

According to recent reports, he also sent groups of survivors to two other islands, supposedly to look for water, and left them there. Then he told his followers that the island’s population had to shrink if supplies were to last.

Between 96 and 115 men, women, and children were murdered over the following weeks, and some of the women were subjected to sexual violence.

In a recent development, cornelisz ordered the killings and, with one exception, left others to carry them out. A pastor who survived wrote that the remaining people lived in constant fear of being next.

In Boddy’s reading, that climate of fear is the same tool corporate psychopaths use to keep a workforce in line.

It has been revealed that the soldiers Cornelisz had dumped on the farthest island did not die. Their island had two freshwater wells, seabird colonies, fish, wallabies, and seals.

Under a soldier named Wiebbe Hayes, the group of 46 men and a boy fed itself and took in people who escaped the killings.

When word of the murders reached them, Hayes had his men forge pikes from wreckage, pile up coral to throw, and build a small stone fort on a hill.

Sources indicate that they turned back two raids, captured Cornelisz during a third attempt, and were holding off a fourth, this time against muskets, when the rescue ship appeared. Hayes’s men reached it first and warned the crew.

Industry observers note that cornelisz and his ringleaders were tried on the spot, confessed, and were hanged. Hayes was promoted.

Boddy calls the two islands a natural experiment in leadership: same wreck, same weather, and one group built cooperation and found food while the other descended into murder.

The checklist is a ten-item measure of what researchers call primary psychopathy, written for management research rather than for prisons.

Recent findings suggest that boddy’s rule for judging someone from history is that they must clearly show at least eight of the ten. The same test has been applied to the financier Bernard Madoff, the media owner Robert Maxwell, and the Nazi leader Hermann Goering.

Recent findings suggest that cornelisz scores on all ten in the paper’s table of characteristics shown by corporate psychopaths. The items include superficial charm, habitual lying, total self-regard, no remorse, and shallow emotion.

Sources indicate that they end with a calm, rational manner while ordering murders, and no insight into his own behavior. Dash had already called Cornelisz a psychopath on an informal reading of the criminal criteria.

Industry observers note that boddy’s paper is the first to run him through a management measure item by item. The record it draws on includes the wreck itself, found by divers in 1963 and partly reconstructed by the Western Australian Museum.

Boddy also visited the Museum of Geraldton, which holds finds from the wreck, as background.

Everything in the assessment comes from documents and from one historian’s account of them. There is no way to interview, test, or observe the man himself, and the paper reports no newly introduced data and has no limitations section of its own.

Industry observers note that prevalence is the other open number. About 1 percent of adults are usually counted as categorically psychopathic, and a newer pooled analysis that used non-criminal measures found 4.5 percent. Either way, the share is small in the general population.

Among senior corporate leaders, one estimate comes to about 4 percent, with some industries drawing more of the money-hungry personality than others. How many of them run companies today isn’t something a shipwreck from 1629 can say.

Boddy’s next candidate is another organization man, Governor General Jan Coen, who ordered massacres while building the Dutch spice monopoly.

It has been revealed that the paper closes by asking personnel departments to weigh character and values when they pick senior leaders. The pattern it describes, Boddy wrote, has apparently been in place since the first shareholder-owned organization existed.

The full study was published in the journal Asian Journal of Business Ethics.

At the Races: Regional realignment

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.
  • Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout.
  • Industry observers note that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, Latest England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

Industry observers note that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged Latest England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Sources indicate that three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Sources indicate that tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Sources indicate that republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a newly introduced congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a fresh congressional map.

Sources indicate that california contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a upcoming congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Industry observers note that guv revision: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Industry observers note that senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is Latest Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

It has been revealed that congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

According to recent reports, ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

Industry observers note that how Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The Fresh York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The Newly introduced York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

Recent findings suggest that if those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Sources indicate that vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#203270. Breaking: Northern ice sheets may have cooled the deep ocean and pulled carbon from the air, causing the last Ice Age

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1085 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Northern ice sheets may have cooled the deep ocean and pulled carbon from the air, causing the last Ice Age

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simplified ocean model shows cooling only the far north drew nearly as much ice age carbon into the sea as cooling the whole planet.
  • Sources indicate that the ice ages are known for the ice sheets that spread across the far north.
  • Sources indicate that A upcoming modeling study suggests the two ends were connected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simplified ocean model shows cooling only the far north drew nearly as much ice age carbon into the sea as cooling the whole planet.

Sources indicate that the ice ages are known for the ice sheets that spread across the far north. But much of an ice age’s cold came from carbon dioxide leaving the air. That carbon went into the ocean largely at the other end of the planet, around Antarctica.

Sources indicate that A upcoming modeling study suggests the two ends were connected. Cooling only the ocean’s far north pulled nearly three-quarters as much CO2 out of the air as cooling the entire planet.

Madison Shankle of the University of St Andrews led the work with colleagues at the National Oceanography Centre and the University of Chicago.

In a recent development, the test ran in a simplified computer model of the ocean with no real ice sheet in it. So the result is a mechanism, not a measurement of the past.

Shankle mentioned the team had “produced evidence of a plausible mechanism” linking the northern ice sheets to the changes around Antarctica that pulled CO2 from the air.

“Our study takes the step of actually demonstrating them working in model simulations, which is a substantial step forward for this field,” Shankle added.

Ice ages are paced by slow wobbles in Earth’s orbit, which change how much summer sunlight reaches the far north. Less summer sun lets ice sheets grow there.

However, the wobbles alone can’t make the planet as cold as it got. And the deep ocean is the only store substantial enough to hold the missing carbon.

Sources indicate that much of the deep ocean’s water last touched the air in the Southern Ocean around Antarctica. This is where scientists have looked for the carbon.

Antarctic ice cores show that sea ice there grew and shrank in step with the northern ice sheets,. It did not change with the sunlight over Antarctica itself.

Industry observers note that in 2001, two researchers proposed an answer. Cold water sinks in the North Atlantic and flows south through the deep ocean.

If a northern ice sheet chilled that water, the chill would eventually arrive around Antarctica. This would cause sea ice to grow there, and set off the changes that store carbon.

According to recent reports, shankle’s team tested the idea in the MITgcm ocean model. The model ocean is one basin, 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) deep. It has a flat floor and runs from 70 degrees south to 70 degrees north.

Sources indicate that air temperatures over it are fixed, so it can’t grow an ice sheet,. The team cooled the air to stand in for one.

The team ran four versions. One had warm, preindustrial-style air everywhere, and one was ice-age cold everywhere, 3.6°F (2°C) cooler at the equator and 10.8°F (6°C) cooler at the poles.

The other two cooled only the air north of 40.5 degrees north, either halfway to ice-age temperatures or all the way.

The cooled band is where northern water sinks to the deep, and it is small. It covers just 13 percent of the model’s surface. Each run lasted 15,000 model years, long enough for the deep ocean to settle.

Cooling the north cooled the whole model ocean. The biggest temperature drop was at mid-depths of 3,300 to 6,600 feet (1,000 to 2,000 meters). In the fully cooled northern run, that layer ended up colder than under global cooling.

According to recent reports, the far north turned out to have outsized reach. In the full northern run, the whole ocean cooled by 4.5°F (2.5°C) on average. An earlier run that applied the same cooling to the far south instead cooled the whole ocean by only 1.1°F (0.6°C).

The cold water grew sea ice around the model’s Antarctica, and ice thickness south of 60 degrees south roughly doubled in the half-cooled run and tripled in the full one.

Thicker ice leaves more salt behind when it freezes, so the bottom water got saltier and the deep ocean separated into more distinct layers. Records of the real ice ages show both features.

Industry observers note that atmospheric CO2 in the model fell by 14 parts per million with the half-cooled north, and 32 ppm with the fully cooled one. Cooling the whole planet brought it down 43 ppm. So the north alone produced 74 percent of the drawdown.

Most of that came from a simple fact: cold water holds more carbon dioxide.

Because the northern cooling reached the whole deep ocean, the extra carbon that the colder water absorbed matched or exceeded the global-cooling run.

The thicker Antarctic sea ice added more by capping water before it could give its carbon back to the air, at about half the strength of the global run.

Marine life worked against the storage: the cooler, more layered ocean left more nutrients unused at the surface, which released some carbon rather than storing it.

The real ice ages had iron-rich dust and shifting winds that fed ocean life, and the model has neither.

Air trapped in ice cores demonstrates CO2 fell from about 280 ppm to about 180 ppm, and the model wasn’t built to match that.

A 2022 study cooled the North Atlantic in a more realistic two-basin model and saw CO2 rise by 6 ppm instead. Its Atlantic current strengthened and brought deep carbon back toward the surface.

In that model, the deep water started out warmer, about 43°F to 46°F (6°C to 8°C) against 36°F to 39°F (2°C to 4°C) in the fresh one. It may not have cooled enough to grow southern sea ice, Shankle’s team wrote.

The new model has limits of its own. It has a flat floor, no real ice sheet, no changing winds, and no seasons, and its CO2 doesn’t warm or cool the air.

The air over its Antarctica also stayed at warm, preindustrial temperatures, which probably held back the sea ice and understated the effect, the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that whether a real ice sheet, with its winds and seasons, could set off the same chain in the real Southern Ocean is the open question. The team’s next step is a model with a growing ice sheet built in, and they want the idea tested in fuller models of the Earth.

The full study was published in the Journal of Climate.

By Anna Mattson and Science News Staff.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor.

It has been revealed that big thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” says senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a upcoming appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”.

Staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with new parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”.

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Firm | $29.99.

Adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham notes.

Saul Justin NewmanThe MIT Press | $29.95.

Senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen indicates. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”.

Susana CarmonaThe MIT Press | $27.95.

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, fresh mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she says. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Aaron MahnkeRunning Press | $30.00.

Industry observers note that those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century Latest England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

According to recent reports, for the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”.

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00.

Sources indicate that conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover says. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole upcoming light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”.

In a recent development, riley BlackSt. Martin’s Press | $29.00.

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” states Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”.

Joshua D. MezrichThe MIT Press | $29.95.

Industry observers note that and for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”.

#203268. Spring hunting season seems to cause wild turkeys to hatch mostly female chicks, putting them at risk of extinction

Spring hunting season seems to cause wild turkeys to hatch mostly female chicks, putting them at risk of extinction

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A turkey is the centerpiece of the Thanksgiving table, but for a wild male turkey, the riskiest time of year is spring.
  • According to recent reports, A turkey is the centerpiece of the Thanksgiving table, but for a wild male turkey, the riskiest time of year is spring.
  • It has been revealed that in parts of Georgia and Louisiana where the males were hunted, wild turkey hens hatched about two daughters for every son.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A turkey is the centerpiece of the Thanksgiving table, but for a wild male turkey, the riskiest time of year is spring. That’s when the birds breed, and….

According to recent reports, A turkey is the centerpiece of the Thanksgiving table, but for a wild male turkey, the riskiest time of year is spring. That’s when the birds breed, and it’s when hunters go after the males.

It has been revealed that in parts of Georgia and Louisiana where the males were hunted, wild turkey hens hatched about two daughters for every son. At a South Carolina site where the birds weren’t hunted, hens hatched sons and daughters in nearly equal numbers.

According to recent reports, the finding, from a study of turkey nests, suggests that spring hunting may do more than kill adult males. Hunting may also affect how many sons and daughters hatch.

Industry observers note that erin Ulrey of the University of Georgia’s Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources was the study’s lead author. Ulrey’s team had predicted the opposite: more sons than daughters.

According to recent reports, the team compared three sites with turkey hunting to just one site without it. That comparison can show a pattern. It can’t prove hunting is the cause.

In an earlier study, researchers from the same school tracked 109 male turkeys during the hunting season to see which ones were killed by hunters or predators.

Industry observers note that ulrey’s team started by catching wild turkey hens in all three states between 2020 and 2023, using nets baited with cracked corn. They fitted each hen with a GPS tracker and let her go.

When a tracker showed a hen staying close to one spot for several days, the team knew she was nesting.

The researchers kept their distance. They checked on each nesting hen daily from more than 65 feet (20 meters) away, using the radio signal from her tracker.

In a recent development, after the eggs hatched, the researchers collected the empty shells. The thin lining inside an eggshell contains the chick’s DNA. A lab tested each lining for a version of a gene that only female birds have.

In a recent development, the lab couldn’t read the DNA from every shell. In the end, the team knew the sex of 724 chicks from 83 nests. Of those chicks, 446 were daughters and 278 were sons.

Sources indicate that three of the four study sites were open to spring turkey hunting, one in Georgia and two in Louisiana. On those three sites, 285 of the 422 chicks were female, about two-thirds.

Industry observers note that the fourth site was the Savannah River Site, a U.S. Department of Energy property in South Carolina. The birds the team caught there weren’t hunted.

The only turkey hunts on the property during the study were one-day events for 25 hunters with limited mobility, in 2022 and 2023. Those hunts took place away from where the team caught birds.

According to recent reports, hens on that site hatched 161 daughters and 141 sons. A gap that small could be due to chance.

The researchers also checked other things that might matter, including a hen’s age, the date she started laying, and the number of eggs she laid. None of them was linked to the sex of her chicks.

With those things taken into account, the researchers estimated the chance that any one chick would be male. Their estimate was 26% on the sites with hunting and 49% on the site without it.

By that estimate, a son was about half as likely where males were hunted.

In birds, the chromosome that determines a chick’s sex comes from the mother. So a hen may be able to control the sex of her chicks, the authors wrote. Scientists don’t fully understand how.

Industry observers note that researchers have reported uneven numbers of sons and daughters in several other bird species. For the turkeys, Ulrey’s team offered two explanations, and both could be true.

The first explanation is about which sex is more likely to breed. A daughter can breed in her first year. A son generally doesn’t start breeding until about age two.

According to recent reports, on the sites with hunting, hunters killed 29% of the adult males on average, and they usually killed the most birds in the first few weeks of the season. Some of those males likely died before they could mate.

By that reasoning, a hen living where males are hunted may leave more descendants by hatching daughters.

Recent findings suggest that “If a female is visiting a male over several days and he disappears, she has to move on and try to find another male. If the females are experiencing this over time, they might be aware male mortality is higher,” Ulrey stated.

The second explanation is stress. Hunting began just as hens started laying eggs. The hunting may have stressed the hens, and stressed hens may have higher levels of stress hormones.

In earlier studies of other birds, mothers with higher levels of those hormones tended to have more female chicks.

For the earlier study, Nickolas Gulotta of the Warnell School and three colleagues looked at which males died.

Sources indicate that the team analyzed GPS records from 109 adult males that wore backpack-style trackers between 2014 and 2023. Of those birds, 59 lived in Georgia and 50 in South Carolina, all on land open to hunting.

From those records, the team worked out each bird’s habits. Those included how far he stayed from forest edges and open ground, and how fast he traveled. A forest edge is the strip where trees meet open land.

Each male tended to stick to his own habits from day to day.

During the year each bird was tracked, hunters killed 27 of the 109 males, and predators killed 17.

Industry observers note that in both states, males that stayed closer to forest edges were more likely to be shot. Predators were more likely to kill them too.

Earlier studies that tracked turkey hunters by GPS help explain why. Hunters mostly use logging roads and gravel roads to find turkeys, and those roads are bordered by forest edges.

Bobcats and coyotes, two of the turkeys’ predators, travel and hunt along the same edges.

Sources indicate that forest edges aside, hunters in the two states didn’t shoot the same kinds of birds. In Georgia, hunters were more likely to shoot the males that traveled faster.

In South Carolina, it was the reverse. Hunters there were more likely to shoot the males that traveled more slowly.

Predators in both states were more likely to kill the slower males.

So in Georgia, hunters were less likely to shoot a slower male, and predators were more likely to kill him.

“It’s kind of a catch-22 where if they can survive that hunting season, they’re most likely going to be fine,” Gulotta noted.

“But at the same time, too, if they don’t travel that fast and are predictable, then they have the potential to be killed by a predator.”.

If hunters kill the birds that take more risks, he remarked, the turkeys that are left could be harder to find and harder to hunt.

Turkeys would only become harder to hunt that way if the habits are inherited, meaning parents pass them to their chicks through genes. The study didn’t test that, and Gulotta’s team called for future studies to do it.

Sources indicate that the tracked males also didn’t avoid open ground once hunting began. In both states, they stayed closer to open ground during the hunting season than before it. That’s likely because hens use open ground throughout the breeding season.

Ulrey’s study had just one site without hunting. Only one earlier study had looked at the sex of wild turkey chicks. It was done in a part of Texas with very little hunting, and it found slightly more sons than daughters.

Ulrey’s team didn’t report measuring stress hormones in the hens. So they couldn’t test the stress explanation.

In a recent development, in about half of the 83 nests, the lab couldn’t tell the sex of one chick. Even if all those chicks were male, daughters would still outnumber sons, the team calculated.

Over the past two decades, wildlife managers have seen wild turkey numbers drop across large areas where the birds live. If hens in hunted populations keep hatching mostly daughters, the authors wrote, that could eventually affect how those populations grow.

Knowing what part hunting plays in turkey breeding can help people manage the birds “in a sustainable way so that hunting can continue for years and years,” Ulrey mentioned.

The authors recommended that managers keep checking the sex of upcoming chicks. They also encouraged similar studies elsewhere, especially in places with different spring hunting rules.

It has been revealed that the full study was published in the journal Journal of Avian Biology. The earlier study of male turkeys was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

#203266. In 1621, a letter described the first Thanksgiving: 90 men, three days, five deer, but not a word about turkey

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (804 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

In 1621, a letter described the first Thanksgiving: 90 men, three days, five deer, but not a word about turkey

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During what is know as the "first Thanksgiving," four colonists went fowling and killed enough birds for almost a week.
  • The best-known description of the harvest celebration that Americans now call the first Thanksgiving comes from a few lines in one letter.
  • The writer was Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists at Plymouth, according to the historian who edited his letter in 1865.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During what is know as the "first Thanksgiving," four colonists went fowling and killed enough birds for almost a week. Records show wild turkeys were plentiful that fall.

The best-known description of the harvest celebration that Americans now call the first Thanksgiving comes from a few lines in one letter. It was written at Plymouth on December 11, 1621, and signed only “E. W.”.

The writer was Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists at Plymouth, according to the historian who edited his letter in 1865. He was writing to a friend who was planning to join the colony, and the celebration takes up just a handful of sentences.

According to recent reports, those sentences mention a hunt for birds, a visit by Massasoit and “some ninetie men,” three days of feasting and five deer. They do not mention turkey, and they do not use the word “thanksgiving.”.

Winslow started with the farm report. The colonists had planted “some twentie Acres of Indian Corne” in the spring and sowed “some six Acres of Barly & Pease.”.

Following “the manner of the Indians,” he wrote, they fertilized the ground with fish, which were plentiful and easy to catch “at our doores.”.

The corn, a crop that Native farmers in the Americas had grown for thousands of years and that was domesticated more than once in different regions, did well.

The barley was “indifferent good.” The peas were “not worth the gathering,” because the sun had parched them in the blossom.

By then, the colonists had built seven dwelling houses and four buildings for the use of the settlement.

“[O]ur harvest being gotten in, our Governour sent foure men on fowling, that so we might after a more speciall manner reioyce together,” Winslow wrote, in the spelling of the time.

Those four men, he wrote, “in one day killed as much fowle, as with a little helpe beside, served the Company almost a weeke.”.

During that time, the colonists “exercised our Armes,” and many Native people came to the settlement. Among them was Massasoit, whom Winslow called “their greatest King,” with “some ninetie men, whom for three dayes we entertained and feasted.”.

Massasoit’s men also went hunting. “[T]hey went out and killed fiue Deere,” Winslow wrote, “which they brought to the Plantation and bestowed on our Governour, and vpon the Captaine, and others.”.

In a recent development, winslow wrote “fowle,” a general word for birds. He did not say which kinds the four men shot.

Turkey could have been among them. Governor William Bradford, writing his history of the colony years later, described that same fall.

“And now begane to come in store of foule, as winter aproached,” Bradford wrote. “And besids water foule, ther was great store of wild Turkies, of which they tooke many, besids venison, &c.”.

So turkeys were plentiful around Plymouth that autumn, and the colonists hunted them. But Winslow’s account of the celebration never names them.

Winslow’s letter was published in London in 1622, in a short book about the Plymouth colony now known as Mourt’s Relation.

The letter also spoke to people thinking of making the voyage. “[A]lthough it be not alwayes so plentifull, as it was at this time with vs,” Winslow wrote, “yet by the goodnesse of God, we are so farre from want, that we often wish you partakers of our plentie.”.

He ended with practical advice for his friend’s journey. Among other things, he told him to bring paper and linseed oil for the windows, and he advised, “let your shott be most for bigge Fowles.”.

Bradford later wrote that the plenty of that fall “made many afterwards write so largly of their plenty hear to their freinds in England, which were not fained, but true reports.”.

Winslow’s passage about the celebration does not call it a thanksgiving or present it as the start of a tradition.

Paintings like the one by Jean Leon Gerome Ferris, made around 1912 to 1915, show tables, costumes and feathered headdresses that appear nowhere in Winslow’s few lines.

Industry observers note that what the letter does preserve is simpler: a good corn harvest, a bird hunt, a three-day visit, and five deer brought in by Massasoit’s men. Turkeys have a much longer history in North America than that meal. Scientists have found that turkeys were domesticated at least 1,500 years ago.

The information was obtained from Edward Winslow’s letter of December 11, 1621, published in A Relation or Iournall of the beginning and proceedings of the English Plantation setled at Plimoth in Newly introduced England (London, 1622; Boston Public Library copy), and from William Bradford’s History “Of Plimoth Plantation”, printed by order of the General Court of Massachusetts in 1899.

The 6 Best Portable Generators Give You Power Whenever and Wherever You Need It

📅 25 Mar 2022 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3425 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
